search_text: responsible travel in gilgit baltistan responsible travel in gilgit baltistan in practice waste water porter welfare photography dress and spending that reaches local families responsible travel local communities leave no trace responsible travel local communities leave no trace travel guides why this matters here gilgit baltistan is a small high fragile place villages sit on irrigated land built by hand over generations water comes from glaciers that are visibly changing waste does not decompose easily at altitude and there is almost no system for removing it tourism has grown quickly and how visitors behave now will decide what the region looks like in twenty years none of what follows is difficult most of it costs nothing waste carry it out there is no rubbish collection on a trekking route and burying waste at altitude does nothing it stays there often for decades on our treks and expeditions the team carries out what it carries in including kitchen waste and packaging what you can do remove excess packaging before you fly carry a small bag for your own wrappers and tissues and resist the urge to leave anything biodegradable behind orange peel does not biodegrade on a glacier in villages and towns the simplest contribution is to avoid single use plastic a refillable bottle removes dozens of bottles from a two week trip water water from the glacier looks clean and often is but it is also the drinking and irrigation supply for the villages below wash at least fifty metres from any stream use biodegradable soap sparingly or none at all and never use detergent directly in running water on trek the camp boils water for the group a filter bottle or purification tablets as backup means you never need to buy bottled water on the road toilets where there is a toilet tent use it where there is not go well away from water and paths dig down and carry out all paper and hygiene products in a sealed bag this is the single most common failure on popular routes and it is the one visitors notice most on arrival at a busy camp porters and staff your trek depends on people carrying loads at altitude responsible operators have agreed load limits provide proper clothing and footwear for high and cold sections provide shelter and food at camp and carry insurance for staff we follow these standards and you are welcome to ask us exactly how they apply on your route what travellers can do keep your duffle within the agreed weight learn a few names do not expect staff to carry personal items beyond the agreement and tip through the guide at the end so it is shared fairly rather than handed out unevenly along the trail photography and people ask before photographing people particularly women and children and accept no gracefully a smile and a gesture toward the camera is usually enough to make the question clear if you promise to send a photograph send it people remember do not give sweets pens or money to children it encourages begging from passing vehicles and undermines school attendance if you want to contribute ask your guide about the local school or health post and give there instead dress and customs gilgit baltistan is relaxed and welcoming and it is also conservative loose clothing covering shoulders and knees is appropriate for men and women alike in villages and towns a scarf is useful for women at religious sites during ramadan avoid eating and drinking openly in public during daylight ask before entering mosques shrines or private courtyards permission is almost always given and asking is what matters spending where it stays the money that helps most is the money that stays in the valley local guest houses family run hotels village cooks local drivers and porters and craft bought directly from the people who made it bargaining hard over small amounts in a village shop saves you very little and costs the seller a great deal choosing a locally based operator has the same effect we are based in skardu our guides drivers and cooks are from these valleys and the wages stay here on the big glacier treks such as the k2 base camp trek and the gondogoro la trek porter welfare matters most before you book with any operator ask about load limits wages insurance and the clothing and shelter porters are given wildlife deosai is home to the himalayan brown bear a protected and still recovering population if you see one stay in the vehicle keep your distance and do not approach or try to attract it for a photograph the same applies to ibex and markhor in the side valleys feeding wild animals and leaving food waste that attracts them to campsites puts both animals and people at risk sacred and sensitive places rock carvings old shrines and ancient buddhist sites are scattered along the indus and the karakoram highway many unprotected do not climb on them mark them or take fragments some areas near borders and sensitive installations have photography restrictions your guide will tell you where and that advice is worth following exactly a short checklist refillable water bottle no single use plastic carry out everything including paper and peel wash away from streams minimal soap ask before photographs no sweets or money to children loose modest clothing in villages tip through the guide fairly and at the end keep your distance from wildlife buy and stay local where you can travelling this way does not make a trip harder it usually makes it better because it opens doors an invitation to tea a conversation a name remembered the next year if you want to know how we work with porters and communities our social responsibility page sets it out and you are always welcome to ask us directly
